answer.text: Each predicate in the program evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: Each clause within a predicate evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: That's Clause Coverage (CC).

answer.text: All combinations of clause truth values are exercised for each predicate

feedback.text: That's Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

answer.text: Every path through the predicate's decision structure is exercised

feedback.text: That describes Path Coverage, not Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Predicate Coverage (PC) only requires the whole predicate to take both truth values at least once; it says nothing about the individual clauses inside it — that finer-grained requirement is Clause Coverage.

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ b, clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b true, p's value is exactly a's value, so toggling a toggles p.
When b is false, p is false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Determination is a per-clause, per-assignment condition, not a constant.
Conjunctions do have determining assignments — just not when b is false.

generalfeedback.text: A clause c determines predicate p when changing only c's truth value changes p's truth value while the other clauses stay fixed. For p = a ∧ b, that happens exactly when b = true: p then mirrors a exactly.

questiontext.text: How does Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC) differ from Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC)?

answer.text: RACC additionally requires the minor clauses to hold identical values in the true/false test pair for the major clause

feedback.text: Correct — RACC is the stricter, "same minor-clause values" version of CACC.

answer.text: RACC drops the requirement that the major clause determines the predicate

feedback.text: That describes General Active Clause Coverage (GACC), not RACC.

answer.text: RACC only counts inactive clauses, not active ones

feedback.text: That describes the inactive-clause family (GICC/CICC), not RACC.

answer.text: RACC requires covering all combinations of clause values

feedback.text: That's Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

generalfeedback.text: Both criteria require, for each major clause ci, a pair of tests where ci determines predicate p once true and once false. CACC allows the other (minor) clauses to differ between that pair; RACC additionally pins the minor clauses to the same values across the pair, making it strictly stronger.

questiontext.text: A predicate has 3 independent clauses. How many tests does Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^3 combinations of true/false.
That's roughly the size of Clause Coverage (one flip per clause), not every combination.
Too few — 4 tests can't realize all 8 truth-value combinations.
6 falls short of the full 2^3 = 8 combinations.

generalfeedback.text: Combinatorial Coverage requires every one of the 2^n truth-value combinations of n clauses to be exercised (subject to feasibility); with 3 independent clauses that is 2^3 = 8 tests.

questiontext.text: CACC (and RACC) is infeasible for a clause that can never determine its predicate.

feedback.text: Correct — if no assignment of the other clauses ever lets that clause determine the predicate, no test can satisfy the active-clause requirement for it.
Determination is a precondition for active-clause coverage; without it the criterion's test requirement for that clause has no test that can satisfy it, so it is infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria (CACC, RACC, GACC) require a test pair where the clause determines the predicate. If some clause structurally never determines the predicate (e.g., it is masked out or redundant), that test requirement can never be satisfied — it is infeasible.

questiontext.text: Which DNF-based logic-coverage criterion requires every unique true point of the predicate to be covered? (acronym)

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

generalfeedback.text: Unique True Point Coverage (UTPC) requires, for each term in the predicate's DNF representation, a test that makes exactly that term true (and all others false) — the "unique" true point for that term.
